previous.passage: Night is honest. In the sanatorium above the lake outside Bergen, I learned that patients say at two in the morning what they hide by daylight. Thorvald, my night patient, could not sleep unless I wheeled him to the end of the dock, where the water lay black and still. On the fourth night he showed me an envelope addressed to his brother, sealed and stamped and eleven years old. He had written it the week after their quarrel. He never mailed it, he said, and his brother had died the following spring. He held it on his blanket while he talked, and I understood that the apology had become an anchor he dragged behind him, slowing every hour he had left. Before dawn he asked me, Sigrid, to keep it for him. I put it in my apron pocket, where it weighed almost nothing.
previous.question: As used in the text, the phrase “an anchor he dragged behind him” most nearly suggests that the unsent apology was
options: a source of steadiness that kept Thorvald calm at night
a memory Thorvald was ready to throw into the lake

previous.explanation: Thorvald는 형과 다툰 뒤 쓴 사과 편지를 11년 동안 부치지 못했고, 형은 이미 세상을 떠났다. 화자는 그 사과가 남은 시간을 늦추며 끌고 다니는 닻이 되었다고 말하는데, 이는 그를 붙잡는 후회의 무게를 뜻하므로 D가 정답이다. A는 닻의 '안정' 의미에 끌린 오답이고, B와 C는 형의 죽음으로 화해의 가능성이 사라졌다는 점과 맞지 않는다. 편지를 Sigrid에게 맡기자 거의 무게가 없었다는 대비도 이 해석을 뒷받침한다.

previous.passage:
Who pays a clockmaker for the hours he gives away?
My father, Santiago, bent above his bench
on Forty-Third Street, where the trains shook dust
from the rafters into every open case.
Ottavio came in winter with a watch
his wife had worn, its mainspring broken, its glass
clouded like a frozen pond.
He counted out his nickels on the counter.
My father pushed them back without a word
and worked past closing, past supper, past the lamps,
spending his minutes like coins on a stranger
while I translated nothing, for nothing needed saying.
When the watch ticked, Ottavio wept in Italian.
My father answered him in Spanish.
I stood between them with my English,
the only one who thought words were required.
previous.question: As used in the text, the phrase “spending his minutes like coins on a stranger” most nearly suggests that Santiago was
options: giving his own time freely in place of taking payment
wasting time carelessly on a repair he did not value

previous.explanation: Santiago는 Ottavio가 내민 동전을 말없이 돌려주고, 가게 문을 닫은 뒤에도 늦게까지 시계를 고친다. 그러므로 '분을 동전처럼 쓴다'는 비유는 돈 대신 자기 시간을 선물처럼 내어 주었다는 뜻이며 A가 정답이다. C는 동전이라는 단어에 끌린 오답이고, B와 D는 정성껏 오래 일한 장면과 어긋난다. 첫 행의 질문도 대가 없이 내어 준 시간이라는 주제를 미리 보여 준다.

previous.passage:
Once, I loved the library on Central Avenue
for its hush, its radiators ticking like patient clocks,
the way Elan would leave me in the stacks
and read the paper by the window, never hurrying.
We had a rhythm there: I chose, he signed.
Then on a Saturday in March he said,
between the atlases and the encyclopedias,
that he had sold the house, that we would move
to Denver in June, that it was settled.
Settled. As if I were a column he had added.
Now the radiators only hiss.
The books lean on each other like strangers in a line.
I, Nayeli, twelve, take down a map
and trace a road I did not choose.

previous.passage: By the seventh evening of the rainy season, Kwesi had climbed the stairs to Obinna's projection booth for the seventh time, carrying the same cracked lens wrapped in cloth. Obinna, who mended everything in the old Accra cinema from ceiling fans to torn film, laughed at him each time. 'A lens is like an egg,' he said. 'Once broken, you may glue it, but you will not hatch anything.' Still Kwesi came, and still Obinna glued, and the townspeople began to joke that the two men were rehearsing a comedy. On the seventh evening, however, Obinna held the lens to the projector's beam and saw, through the crack, the screen below split into two pictures, one bright and one dim. He did not laugh. He asked Kwesi whose face had been in the last film shown through it. Kwesi answered that it was his late mother's, and Obinna set down his glue and said nothing for a long time.
previous.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone in the text?
options: From lighthearted mockery of Kwesi's visits to solemn, respectful understanding.
From suspicious hostility toward Kwesi to warm, comic friendship between the men.
From tense urgency about the damaged lens to relieved celebration of its repair.
From reverent awe at the cinema's history to playful teasing about its machines.
previous.explanation: 앞부분에서 Obinna는 매번 웃으며 깨진 렌즈를 달걀에 비유하고, 마을 사람들은 두 사람이 희극을 연습한다고 농담한다. 그러나 'however' 이후 Obinna는 웃지 않고 렌즈에 비친 마지막 얼굴을 묻고, 그것이 Kwesi의 돌아가신 어머니였다는 답에 오래 침묵한다. 따라서 가벼운 조롱에서 엄숙한 이해로 바뀐다는 A가 정답이다. B와 D는 변화의 방향을 거꾸로 제시하고, C는 수리의 성공을 축하하는 장면이 없으므로 틀리다.

previous.passage: We found the letters in a biscuit tin beneath the workbench of our mother's radio repair shop in Marrakesh, a week after the funeral. My brother Yiannis read them aloud while I, Yasmin, sorted vacuum tubes into egg cartons. Most were from a man identified only by an initial, thanking her for fixing his radio without charge, again and again, for eleven years. Yiannis grew quiet; I knew what he was thinking. A free repair every month starts to look like a secret. __Then I remembered how she used to leave a radio playing by the shop door at night, turned low, tuned to the station that read the news for the blind.__ I went back through the tin and found, at the bottom, a receipt from a school for the blind, signed with the same initial. Our mother, I think now, was not hiding anything; she was simply listening for someone.

previous.passage: On the first Tuesday of every month, I collected my younger brother Wolfram from the reading room of a quiet library near the Ringstrasse in Vienna, where his tutor, Anselm, taught him geography from maps older than our grandparents. I disliked Anselm at first. He was late, he hummed, and he insisted that Wolfram learn to walk home by landmarks rather than by the tram map I had drawn for him. I thought it was vanity, an old man's romance with the city. Then one winter evening the trams stopped in a snowstorm. I found Wolfram already halfway home, steering by the green dome of a church, the bakery with the brass pretzel, the fountain with the missing nose. He had not needed my map at all. I still think Anselm hums too much. But I no longer think his lessons were for show, and I have started, a little grudgingly, to notice landmarks myself.

Amused indifference, as she treats his lessons as harmless but ultimately pointless.

previous.passage:
Joaquin, I am writing from the bench outside my father's ticket booth at the ferry terminal in Seville, where you stood last Sunday and asked me, quite seriously, how people here say goodbye. I laughed at you then, and I am sorry, but you must understand that nobody had ever asked me before. You had a list from a guidebook: the kiss on each cheek, the handshake, the wave from the deck. You wanted to do it properly. I told you there was no proper way, which was unkind, because there is, and you found it without me. When the horn sounded, you did not kiss or wave. You simply stood at the rail until the ferry turned the bend, the last passenger still facing the dock. My father says only fishermen and homesick people do that. I hope you will write and tell me which you are.

Marisol

previous.passage: Who decides which child stays behind when the olives must be carried down? So the old tellers on the terraces above Naples begin this tale. A young teacher named Emilio came to the hill school and announced that the slowest reader would stay to tend the trees while the others went to market. Alessia, who read slowly but counted quickly, folded her arms and said nothing. On market day Emilio found the baskets tallied wrong and the prices muddled, for no one else could reckon so well, and he climbed back up the hill red-faced to fetch her. The tellers say he never again chose by a single measure, though they add, with a wink, that he took a long time to admit it aloud. Even now, grandmothers who repeat the story pause here to slice bread, and the children wait, chins on hands, for the ending they already know.
